name: chinesename (Chinese name statistics)
note: Chinese given names and surnames, from the data behind a name generator rather than
from a register. China publishes no open name frequencies, and the two datasets that
have the right shape are both NonCommercial -- ChineseNames (CC BY-NC-SA) has the
2,614 given-name characters with frequencies by gender, and the Harvard deposit
(CC BY-NC-ND) has a million given names with gender counts. Neither composes with
Apache-2.0, and no amount of wanting them changes that.
What is taken here is `popular.txt`: the 500 commonest full names with the number of
people holding each. That is an aggregate count and not a roster, the same shape as
the US Census surnames -- which matters, because the best-licensed Chinese corpus
available is Apache-2.0 and is 1.14 million full names of real people. Decoy refuses
rosters, and refused one for Urdu on the same grounds.
Given names are recovered by stripping a known surname off each full name and summing
the counts, which yields 131 names carrying real population weights. Thin, and honest:
these are the names China actually uses most, so a drawn fixture looks like a Chinese
person rather than like a random walk through a dictionary.
No gender. `popular.txt` records how many people hold a name and not who they are, so
the names land on `person.first_name.generic`. Splitting them by guessing which look
feminine would be authoring a claim the source does not make.
`surnames.txt` replaces what Wikidata gave `zh_CN`, which was 41 entries of which nine
were romanisations (`Ning`, `Hung`), three were labels ending in the character for
'surname' rather than surnames, and most of the rest were rare compounds -- 万俟,
南郭, 司空 -- because those are the ones an encyclopaedia finds notable. Drawing from
it produced the Chinese equivalent of an English fixture set where everybody is called
Featherstonehaugh.
Only the 745 single-character surnames are taken. The 212 compound ones are mostly
ancient or non-Han (阿伏干, 阿勒根), and the file carries no frequencies to tell those
apart from 欧阳 and 司马, which are ordinary. Losing a handful of real compound
surnames is the better error.
Unweighted, therefore, for the surnames: the file is a list of what exists. That is a
real weakness -- 王, 李 and 张 cover a fifth of China between them and here they are
as likely as any other -- and it is recorded rather than papered over with an invented
distribution. A frequency table would fix it; none is available under a licence that
composes.
